en: [B22b-2] Thus, having taken the *vakula* garland and waiting for Lavaṅgikā who has arrived, Mālatī has ascended the palace and remains there with her gaze fixed upon her path. And Makaranda, having vowed, "In this matter, the venerable Kāmandakī is our refuge," has gone toward Kāmandakī to relate these events. While matters stand thus, the two maidservants enter.
(1) One [maid]: Friend, you were standing near the music hall with Avalokitā as your only companion, whispering something to yourself.
"Halā" is an address to a maidservant. "Parisare" means in the vicinity.

Friend, it seems that the entire incident concerning Madanodyāna was reported to the Venerable Lady by that friend of Mādhava, Makaranda. Thereupon, desiring to see the young mistress, the Venerable Lady sent Avalokitā on the pretext of some business. I too told her that the young mistress is staying in a secluded spot with Lavaṅgikā as her companion.

The meaning is that Kāmandakī, having learned of Mādhava’s dire condition from Makaranda’s mouth, has dispatched Avalokitā to ascertain Mālatī’s news in order to discover the proper opportunity for a plan to bring about their reunion.
First [Act]: Friend, Lavaṅgikā did not come from the Madanodyāna garden itself, as she was gathering *kesara* flowers. Has she arrived now?
*Kesara* refers to the *vakula* tree. After the word "iti," the verb "having done" (*kṛtvā*) is to be supplied.
Second [interjection]: "Then what?
means "It is exactly so.
Having seized her by the hand as she was indeed falling down, the young mistress of the house, having forbidden her attendants, ascended to the upper terrace.

The word *parā* precedes *patiḥ* and, by its own power, expresses haste (*tvarām*). (2) Therefore, the meaning is "coming quickly. Being quick due to having accomplished one's purpose is the inherent nature of a messenger. "On top of the *alindaka*" means "above the *alindaka*. *Alindaka*: another outer hall. (3) In the reading *uparitalam*, it means "the upper," *talam*: the surface; that is, the window (*vātāyanam*).
FIRST: Surely she is diverting herself with conversation about that high-souled man.
Second [Act]: Whence can she have confidence? By this extraordinary vision today, her obsession will reach its ultimate limit. Obsession (*abhiniveśa*) means attachment (*āsakti*).
In this Kali age, because of Nandana, the Great King, having requested the hand of the princess, was informed by his minister: (4)
First [question]: What does "vijñapta" mean? It means "informed.
(5) Second [statement]: "O Great King, you have power over your own daughters. From this, I infer that Mālatī’s love for Mādhava has indeed become a thorn [in her side] until death.
It is like a thorn, because it causes unbearable pain.
"Even the Blessed One" (prathamā api nāma bhagavatī)—she may perhaps demonstrate some aspect of her blessedness here.
"Api nāma" is used in the sense of possibility.
Second [Enter Mālatī]: O you whose desires are unfulfilled, come.

(6) [Mālatī], having been informed by Lavaṅgikā of the entire account ending with her acceptance of the request for the *vakula* garland, and being filled with longing to hear the subsequent events, asks: "Hum! Friend, what happened after that?"
"Hum" is an indeclinable used for inquiry.
Lavaṅgikā: Therefore, this *vakula* garland was brought by that noble one.
Mālatī: Indeed, it has been fashioned so as to be unevenly fastened on one side.
In the reading *ekovāse*, it means "in one place.
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, you alone are at fault for her lack of delight [here]. (7) According to another reading, it is "for her lack of delight" (*cāramaṇīyatve*) in this case. (8)
Mālatī: How so?
Lavangikā: By him, whose limbs are charmingly dark, who was thus rendered bewildered.
"Mugdha" means fresh and lovely. In the reading "duvvāsāmalaṅga," it means one whose limbs are as dark as *dūrvā* grass. "Vihasta" means agitated or distressed.
Mālatī: Dear friend Lavaṅgikā, you are always so inclined toward offering consolation.

Lavaṅgikā: Friend, what sort of "inclination toward consolation" is there here? Did I not say that he too was directly perceived by you—watching with eyes that possessed the grace of full-blown white lotuses tossed by a gentle breeze, which were restrained under the pretext of arranging a *vakula* garland you had begun; his creeper-like brows dancing with the playful movement of long, steady, and wide-ranging glances born of burgeoning wonder, skillfully mimicking the grace of the deer of the God of Love?

*Paryastam*: surrounded; that is to say, impelled. Regarding *vibhramehiṃ*, since it is a rule of Prākṛta that the plural is used for the dual, the plural form is employed where the dual should have been used. (9) *Balāmoḍi* means force or compulsion; this is a regional term (*deśī*). (10) By means of the pretext of weaving a *vakula* garland, although they had been brought under restraint, their [eyes] spread wide by force; by their creeper-like brows, which were made to dance—that is, made to twerk—there was a mocking of the God of Love’s *sāraṅga* [deer].

"Beholding his archery—that is, observing his graceful gestures (*vilāsa*) exactly as they occur"—this is what must be understood by the word "you. Therefore, the sense is: "Since the intended beauty of the *vakula* garland has not been successfully executed due to the deficiency of your gaze, the fault lies with you alone.

Mālatī: Ah, dear friend, are those graceful gestures of that noble-souled one—which appear for a mere moment—naturally inclined toward causing separation in people who happen to be near him at that time? Or is it as my dear friend suspects?

"Yes," he says, using an interrogative intonation (*kākū*) to signify his acceptance of the fact that [her character] has been made manifest through such observation. For character is to be discerned through long-term association; however, a person who is present for only a moment suspects *vipralambha*—that is, deception—in every case. The meaning is that she fears, "He might deceive me by means of this behavior. Alternatively, where the reading is *ādu* instead of *atha vā*, the sense is *āhosvit*.
Lavaṅgikā: Were you yourself, by your very nature, made to dance without music on that occasion?
Mālatī: Hum. And then what? And then what?

"Hum" [expresses] a lover’s anger. (11) LAVANGIKĀ: Then, having returned, while he was hidden by the bustle of the departing procession, I went to Mandārikā’s house. Indeed, her picture-board had been placed in my hands at dawn.
"Hastīkṛtam" means "entrusted as a deposit."

Mālatī: For what reason? Lavangikā: Indeed, a follower of Mādhava named Kalahaṃsaka desires her. She will show her to him. Consequently, Mandārikā has become a bearer of pleasant news. "Pleasant" should be understood as "to me. Furthermore, this is a slight hint of irony: she is a bearer of news concerning Mādhava, who is dear to Mālatī; for instance, from the drawing of Mālatī’s portrait, it appears that he too is in a state of longing. (12)
Mālatī: Surely that Kalahaṃsaka must have shown that portrait to his own master. Friend, what now would be pleasing to you?

Lavaṅgikā: This is indeed your portrait, which provides for a mere moment a cooling relief to the heart of him who is tormented—tormented by the unbearable distress of being possessed by an unattainable desire, and who himself causes such torment to others.

For him—who is tormented by the thought of seeing you, who causes you torment, and who possesses an intense longing and persistence for you who are so difficult to attain—your portrait serves as a means of cooling his heart for even a moment as it burns with passion. This is one type of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For even this sight of the reflection of Mālatī is indeed dear to her, in that it becomes the cause for the pacification of Mādhava’s torment.

But as for this portrait of him who torments you—which was painted by him while he himself was tormented—it serves as a momentary relief for your heart when it is burning with the intensity of longing for him, who is so difficult to attain.
(13) Mālatī: Oh! Even now my heart remains unattached, since I suspect that even such a consolation is but a deception.
"Anāsaṅga" means lack of confidence or lack of reassurance.

And how about the words? O fortunate one, your speech is indeed observed to be worthy of your physical form in its sweetness. But as for this sight, it is enchanting at the moment yet dreadful in its long-term consequences of suffering. Truly blessed are those women who do not behold you, or who have mastery over their own hearts.
"Worthy" (*sadṛśa*): your appearance is indeed sweet and lovely, and your speech is likewise endowed with the quality of sweetness. "Ammakāḥ": women; this is a regional term (*deśī*).
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, why is it that you have no comfort even in this way?
Mālatī: Friend, how so?

Lavaṅgikā: Friend, he for whose sake you wither away—like a *kaṅkelli* sprout whose bonds have been uprooted, unable to endure the jasmine blossoms—has himself been made aware by the divine Love of the unbearable nature of your torment.

*Bandhana* (binding): the contact between sprouts, stalks, and branches. *Kaṅkelli*: the *aśoka* tree. *Nissahā* (helpless): incapable of endurance. "You are being diminished" (*parihīyase*): you are being led toward decline; thus, the stage of love known as emaciation (*tanutā*) has been described.
Mālatī: May it be well with that noble-souled one now. For me, however, consolation is difficult to obtain—especially today, my friend.

And the recourse to Sanskrit here is due to the expectation that the final moment is imminent, because the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from prior practice of Prakrit manifests, leading to the recollection of Prakrit; for it is well known in the world that such recollection at that time results in birth in an inferior womb, or else it is for the purpose of demonstrating one's skill in the arts (*kalā*).

[1] He reveals that very same apprehension regarding the departure [from existence] with the words "the disease of the mind" (*manoroga*). "The disease of the mind" means mental anguish (*ādhi*); it is incessant and disruptive (*pramāthī*), meaning it causes agitation. Just as a potent poison spreads gradually through the bodily constituents such as the skin, so too does it spread through the limbs in that manner. By this process, it is said that agitation pervades all the limbs. Then, that very agitation, having assumed the form of a burning fever, like a fire that has been fanned into flame, blazes forth without smoke.

It becomes enveloped in garlands of flames. Then that torment strikes and afflicts every limb here and there, like a great fever. The meaning is this: this mental anguish has reached such a state that it cannot be remedied by you unless you abandon that lord of my life. Or rather, my father is not able to protect me, insofar as he does not give me to Mādhava after uniting me with Nandana; nor is my mother, since she does not restrain him while he behaves in such a manner.

Thus, as these two converse, what can even you do? By including Lavaṅgikā—who is on equal footing with her father and mother—under the term "your ladyship," there is an expression of equality intended to grant her the freedom to reveal her own opinion. For mental suffering rooted in physical affliction may be remedied by medicines and the like, but when it is contrary [to such means], it is incurable. [1]

Lavaṅgikā: It is even so. Meetings with the virtuous bestow immediate happiness, yet they are difficult to endure when out of sight. (14) For you, whose physical condition was such that—merely by seeing him for a moment from within a window—the rising of the full moon, appearing like a fire of extraordinary intensity, threatened your life through the cruel operations of love; that very person, having now attained this extraordinary sight, causes you to suffer today. What more need be said here? Therefore, dear friend, this is truly praiseworthy.
We know only this: that for one living in the world of mortals, union with a beloved who is as highly fortunate as one’s own deep affection is the fruit of a rare wish.

What more can there be here? The meaning is that this is entirely appropriate. For him whose very indistinct sight bestows the nature of fire upon the moon and bears fruit through the danger to his life, what wonder is there that his distinct sight, in the manner you have described, produces such torment? By the moon’s bestowal of the nature of fire, the loss of sleep is implied. This is the wish regarding that which is difficult to attain.

We know only this much: its fruit is a meeting with a beloved who is worthy of praise and corresponds to one's deep affection. Regarding the rest of the matter, others must be consulted. The use of the plural "we know" (*jānīmaḥ*) contains this underlying meaning: that the only utility for friends is the bringing about of such a union with a beloved. Just as Uṣā’s friend Citralekhā brought Aniruddha [to her], so shall I also cause you to meet him. (15) Mālatī: Friend, you who propose such a rash act against the life of my beloved Mālatī, begone!
*Dayitam*: the beloved. *Apehi*: depart.

"For a maiden to resolve upon bringing disgrace upon her esteemed family is indeed a great act of recklessness. But Uṣā—having obtained a union with Aniruddha in a dream through the grace of Gaurī, and having determined that every aspect of her approaching union with her beloved was beyond reproach—is at peace; thus, even by acting in this way, she does not commit such an offense. [Speaking thus with tears, she continued: "Or rather, it is I who am at fault here, for though I gaze upon him again and again, my fortitude is maintained only with difficulty, while my heart melts away from afar due to its shyness, making me light through my ill-bred conduct."
"By whom"—the ellipsis implies—"by whom such a resolution to propose such a rash act as yours was formed.
Nevertheless, dear friend:

although one should have said "let it rise," she says "let it blaze" in accordance with her own experience. "With unbroken digits" means complete. This is an outburst of disregard for her own life on the part of one exhausted by the force of the pain of love, which is utterly unbearable. To the question, "Why is Mādhava himself—not the remedy for all her afflictions—not pursued? she replies: "But for me, father—meaning my father—is beloved—meaning not to be abandoned—and praiseworthy."

The meaning is that he is the object of praise for all, consisting as he does of glory; his mother is beloved and his family is beloved, but this Mādhava is not merely one who lies upon the couch of my heart. Now, one might object that abandoning the very person for whose sake this undertaking was begun would produce a contradiction between what precedes and what follows; therefore, he says "not so. It is better to abandon the two of us—whose lives are dear because we are born of two distinguished lineages—than to cast the reproach of blame upon our parents and their families.
[2] Lāvaṅgikā: What means is there now in this matter?

Here, by chance, the sentence of Lavaṅgikā is connected with the reply given by the female door-keeper; this serves to construct the *gaṇḍa*, a constituent element of the dramatic juncture (*saṃdhi*).
(16) Female Door-keeper: This is the venerable lady Kāmandakī. Both: Is it the venerable lady? [B26b]

Because the speech of the female doorkeeper is incomplete without an action, there arises a desire to know that [action]. However, the introduction of an action in that very context serves to establish the connection with the status of a subsequent sentence.
Doorkeeper: I have come to see the mistress of the house.
Both: Then why is there this delay?
Lavaṅgikā: It has indeed become perfectly composed;
the sense is that at this very moment there shall be a meeting with Kāmandakī.

[Kāmandakī]: Regarding the phrase "in both worlds": first, there is no conflict with this world because the King’s anger is not provoked by not openly refusing him. She herself will later explain the lack of conflict with the next world, since she avoids uttering a falsehood by using a general statement: "You are the master over my own daughters, but not over others. (17) As for Vakulāvalī, who was sent by Mādhava into Lavaṅgikā's hand, and the picture-board which was brought by Kalahaṃsaka;

Such indeed was the union and the arrangement between those two. Regarding the "act of giving a daughter" (dārakarma): it refers to marriage. "Supreme" (parārdhya): most excellent. "Consequence" (anubandha): sexual pleasure. "Prosperity" (ṛddhi): the arising of all auspiciousness.
This is Avalokitā; she is Mālatī.

[Kāmandakī] [3]: Kāmandakī speaks of the stage of love known as *tanutā* (emaciation), saying "excessively" (*nikāmam*). Possessing the physical transformations caused by the agony of Love which betrays her passion for Mādhava, she delights the mind through its readiness to achieve the desired end, yet she makes it tremble due to the inability to endure the pangs of passion and the delay caused by the failure to unite with him despite the passing of time. "Excessively" (*nikāmam*) means "to an extreme degree. By the word "interior" (*garbha*), there is an indication of an extreme paleness and delicacy. She is described as such because her form has but a single digit remaining. "Uddāha" means an intense burning. [3]

[4] "Pāṃśulam" means rough. Even though her cheeks and face are pale and rough, she is heart-stealing because, for a person who is exceedingly desirable, even such a state as this constitutes a charming and desired manifestation of love. [4]

[5] *Nīvī* is the binding of the garment on a woman’s hips; its *ucchvasana* is the loosening of that knot. *Dorviṣāda* is the lack of strength in the arms. *Masṛṇam* means slowly. *Mukulam* means sweetly inclined toward closing. *Ākekaram* means with the pupils slightly turned upward. *Snigdham* means expressing affection. *Mugdham* means lovely, or motionless due to being immersed in bliss. (18) Because they have the shape of buds, the breasts themselves are called *mukula*s.

In these two, there is an uninterrupted flow (*utprabandha*), which is a continuous trembling (*vepathu*). *Mūrcchanā* is a state of fainting (*moha*), yet there is intermittent consciousness as well. This is the characteristic sign of the attainment of emotion (*bhāva*), well known through such descriptions as "with relaxed limbs," "closing the eyes," "hair standing on end," and "falling into a state of sleeplessness" (*vinidratām ita*). (19) [5] Mālatī: "O Blessed One, I bow to you.
The phrase "I bow" (*vandāmi*) follows the Buddhist tradition of salutation toward one who has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), just as Śaivas say "Salutation to Śiva" (*namaḥ śivāya*).
Lāvaṅgikā: A well-prepared seat. Mālatī: Is the Blessed One well?

Lāvaṅgikā: This is indeed the prologue to a drama of deception. (Aloud: The speech of the Blessed One is truly extraordinary; it seems as though its exit is obstructed by a throat choked and faltering with heavy tears. What, then, could now be the cause of her distress?
Bāṣpa: tears. Stambha: obstruction. Mantharita: slowed down. Kāmandakī-paricaya: acquaintance. Lavaṅgikā: How so?
Kāmandakī: Victorious—that which is characterized by victory. Spouse—the husband.
Lavaṅgikā: It is said that because of the king’s command, the minister has betrothed Mālatī to Nandana; for this reason, everyone despises the minister.
Mālatī: How have I been made an offering by my father to the king?

Just as someone, having offered a goat or similar animal as a sacrifice to a fierce deity such as Caṇḍikā, accomplishes his own desired end, so too does my father wish to accomplish his own purpose by making me an offering; thus, perceiving it to be equivalent to death, I said, "I have been made an offering," and not that "I have been made a gift. [Mālatī] [7] *Kuṭila* means one whose primary characteristic is deception. *Niṣṇātam* means immersed. *Aidamparyam* means possessing the intended significance regarding this particular meaning.
[7] *Mālatī*: Indeed, the propitiation of others is highly esteemed by my father, but not Mālatī herself.
Lavaṅgikā: It was exactly as the lady commanded; otherwise, why did the minister not consider that this boon would result in one who is difficult to behold and whose youth has passed?
Mālatī: Alas! I am destroyed, an unfortunate woman upon whom the thunderbolt of calamity has fallen.
Lavaṅgikā: Therefore, may the lady be gracious; protect my dear friend from this life-and-death crisis. To you, too, she is truly a daughter.

Life itself is like death because it is devoid of purpose and abounds in suffering; this is "life-and-death. [Kāmandakī] The word *kalpa* is used to indicate that what is ostensibly not to be taught is, in fact, being taught. The meaning here is that the state of not being taught is not complete [in its application]. [8] The phrase "for a dear friend" indicates an excess of affection. He is "difficult to behold" due to old age and ugliness. "Grasper of smoke" refers to Rāhu. He too is difficult to behold, because his gaze causes pain. [8]
Mālatī: Alas, father! Even you have thus [fallen]; everything is utterly conquered by the thirst for worldly enjoyment.
"Thus"—you show no consideration toward me. Avalokitā: The venerable lady has delayed too long. Indeed, I said that the noble Mādhava’s body was unwell.
"Therefore, let us go quickly. This is an introductory remark for the description of Mādhava’s greatness and noble lineage.
Lavaṅgikā says "Aside" (*janāntika*), meaning she speaks softly into the ear:
"Friend Mālatī, we have now learned from the presence of the Holy Lady (the Goddess) the origin of that noble-souled one."
*Udgamaḥ*: origin; source.
*Mālatī*: "In that very way"—the word "only" (*eva*) from the *janāntika* (aside) is carried over here.
"Friend, I have a curiosity."
"Ask," is the intended meaning.
Lavaṅgikā: Who is this person named Mādhava, for whose sake the Blessed Lady maintains her self with such heavy affection?
Regarding the word "yasya" (for whom): the word "kṛte" (on account of) is to be supplied.
LĀVANGIKĀ: Even so, let the lady speak; may she show us favor.
[KĀMANDAKĪ]: Praised men are the very best of men. "Mahānīya" means worthy of worship. "Satīrthya" means similar.

[9] "Vyatikaritāḥ" means pervaded. "Ūrjasvalānām" means of the powerful. Those whose greatness is not measured are such [men]. "Maṅgalānām" refers to the accomplishments of one's goals. "Ketana" means a house. [9]
Mālatī: Friend, my father indeed remembers him at all times by the name bestowed upon him by the Holy Lady (the Goddess).

Here, although one ought to say "Devarāta," the expression "by the name bestowed upon him by the Holy Lady" is used because he has been accepted as her husband; for one should not utter the personal name when referring to a preceptor.
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, people who were present at that time are whispering that they acquired their learning together.

[Kāmandakī] [10] "He alone"—this expresses his abundance through his authority over the sovereignty of all people. "By the radiance of his qualities," meaning by their pervasive expansion; "splendid," meaning praiseworthy. And for those possessing eyes—those who traverse the surface of the earth—he arose as a cause of great festival; he has emerged. For the moon, too, is indeed "splendid" (sundaraḥ), meaning lovely, by that radiance which possesses shimmering qualities; it is possessed of digits and is a delight to the eyes and face. Like the young moon, he is a "young moon" (bālacandra).
[10] Lavaṅgikā: Friend, could it possibly be Mādhava?

[Kāmandakī] [11] *Avikalaḥ*: complete. *Madhuraḥ*: charming. *Unmādataralaiḥ*: flickering due to the onset of passion. *Ālokasthāne*: in a place where he is visible while standing. *Kuvalayitam*: variegated with blue lotuses. [11] Mālatī: "Friend, did you hear that?
Lavaṅgikā: "Just so," said in order to draw her aside in private (*janāntika*).
Friend, from where else could the *pārijāta* tree arise except from the great ocean?
[Kāmandakī]: *Atipātaḥ* means taking away; that is to say, seizing.

[12] *Kṣipan*: driving away. *Madanakalahaḥ*: sexual union; its *chedaḥ*: cessation. *Vihagāḥ*: ruddy geese (*cakravāka*). For they become full of longing at the time of evening due to their imminent separation. *Teṣām*, *mithunam*: a pair consisting of a male and female. *Saudhānām*: of palatial white mansions. *Alaghuṣu*: in extensive, *nikuñjeṣu*: secluded groves. *Ghanatām*: a state of density, meaning persistence for a long duration. *Anibhṛtaḥ*: spreading forth. [12]

Mālatī: How have I been made an offering by my father to the King? Indeed, the service of others is what is weighty for my father, and not Mālatī. Alas, father! Even you, alas, are thus! In every way, the thirst for worldly enjoyment has triumphed. How can he be so high-minded, even though born of a great lineage! My dear friend has spoken well: "For where could the *pārijāta* tree spring from, were it not from the great ocean? Might I perhaps see him once again?
Lavaṅgikā: Avalokitā, this way, this way; let us descend by means of this courtyard.
(A courtyard is a four-winged building.)

[Kāmandakī: The burden has been lightened; much has been accomplished. [13] Now, she briefly demonstrates the sequence of her own activities that have passed, beginning with the words "vare 'nyasmin" ("in another suitor"). *Vicikitsā* means hesitation or reluctance. *Purāvṛttodgārāḥ* refers to discourses on ancient history (*itihāsa*). *Padavī* means path. *Māhātmyam* means greatness. *Abhijanataḥ* means by lineage or family. *Atha* (then) means immediately thereafter. *Vidheh* means of the Creator. *Vidheyaḥ* means that which is to be performed. *Paricayaḥ* means acquaintance or association. Thus ends the statement regarding the remaining duties to be performed by the female messenger. [13] May there be prosperity. The Second Act.
End of the first act. [From here until "khalv iyam viracitā" (defective in C = from B 22b-2 to 23a-10):
*īkṣamāṇā* (ego); *īkṣamāṇā* (B).
*cedyoḥ* (ego); *cedyaḥ* (B).
saṃgītakaśālā° ego : saṃgītaka B; °dvitīyā ego : dviyā B;
draṣṭu° ego : draṣṭa B.
°nimittam ego : nivṛttim B; bhartṛdārikā ego : om. B;
°duravasthayā ego : durdurāvasthayā B.
saṃghaṭṭanopayikaḥ (ego); saṃghaṭṭanopayikaḥ (B) cinomīti (ego); cinomīti kṛtvā (B) parijanaḥ (ego); parija (B)
°svabhāvaḥ (ego): svabhāvaḥ (B); uparitanam (ego): uparitalam (B);
PRATHAMĀ (ego): om. (B).
This "ego" (ahaṃkāra) belongs to her;
this "ego" [is used] in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*); [the word] *iti* is added after *saṃbhāvanāyāt*. B.
°vṛttāntayā ego : vṛttāntā B °samutkaṇṭhayā ego : samutkaṇṭayā B tataḥ ego : tata B
Lāvaṅgikā alone: "This [girl] has been brought here by Lavaṅgikā" (ego: *bhāvena upanītā*); "this [girl] has been led away by her disposition" (B).
"Beside her" (ego: *pārśve*); B: *pāśve*.
Indeed, this [work] was composed by the cowherd C;
C: *vivacanā* B. Ekkovāseti C: ekkaivayāseti B.
Lavaṅgikā alone: Lavaṅgikā.
Here, in the sense of "not being delightful," *atra* [is used]; in the sense of "delightfulness," *atra* [is used].
Mālatī. B: Mālatī; C: Māla.
In what way? Like whom? Lavaṅgikā: By whom that one with a charmingly dark-limbed body was thus rendered bewildered.
